dropped.quote: Maybe causing an existential catastrophe is easier, or quicker, than accelerating world GWP growth. Both seem plausible to me.

dropped.quote: As a proud, self-proclaimed, “nerd,” I, too, love a good science fiction story. However, one goal of my testimony today is to demystify some of these wild claims for you.

dropped.quote: Nothing human makes it out of the near-future.

dropped.quote: If AI doesn't kill us, it will certainly render us incapable of understanding what reality is.

dropped.quote: So you can talk about existential risk and there is existential risk of nuclear war. There's existential risk of bioweapons or dangerously engineered bioweapons, maybe of AI and killer robots or autonomous weapon systems guided by AI.

dropped.quote: Hype and doom, in other words, are two sides of the same (bit)coin.

dropped.quote: My prediction is that companies in the AGI space will have to make a number of high risk decisions as the technology’s capability increases, each time rolling the dice on whether their system has crossed the threshold where it’s actually dangerous.

dropped.quote: Yet these promises are far from bearing fruit and economic analysis increasingly suggests these directions for technology may play a key role in explaining that failure.

dropped.quote: Killer AI is already here, and it’s called drones. And every country is pursuing it. So it’s not the image generators and chatbots one needs to worry about.

dropped.quote: By “catastrophic risks,” I refer to extremely damaging events caused by human misuse or abuse of an advanced AI system. I do not refer to existential risks, or the notion that the AI itself will have a desire to kill or enslave humanity.
dropped.why: He defines his term 'catastrophic risks' as human misuse and sets existential risk aside. That is scoping a term, not a claim that misuse deserves more attention than autonomous AI. Leans hold. No better quote in the passage.

dropped.quote: But the improper use of AI systems can erode deterrence, create destabilizing effects, and reinforce systems of political control and social engineering.
dropped.why: Only says that improper use of AI is a risk. Nothing ranks it above, or sets it against, autonomous superintelligence. No better quote in the passage.

dropped.quote: Maybe it doesn't become a godlike intelligence, which is some of the sort of futuristic transhumanist nonsense. But it could just be this autonomous weapon system on a drone where we want to make them autonomous, because if you have a human in the loop, the human gets jammed.
dropped.why: Hedged ('maybe it doesn't become a godlike intelligence') and embedded in his summary of the effective-altruist argument he says is winning. The alternative he names is autonomous weapons. Elsewhere he raises 'the larger existential risk point'. Leans hold, not a clear stance.

dropped.quote: And so why should we restrict free speech to biological intelligences only?

dropped.quote: The main danger here is precisely that we might refuse to grant AIs their freedom out of fear.
dropped.why: Argues against enslaving AIs, but the reasons given are prudential (a revolt could be destructive, freedom is cheap to grant), not that AIs merit rights. A reader could fairly say he takes no position on whether they deserve moral consideration.

dropped.quote: If we’re lucky, consciousness is a basic feature of information processing and anything smart enough to outcompete us will be at least as conscious as we are.
dropped.why: A hopeful conditional ('if we're lucky') that advanced AI would be conscious, offered as a condition for accepting AI successors. It implies moral consideration would follow, but he never says AIs may merit rights or moral consideration, and the same section says existing AIs have nothing like brain waves.

dropped.quote: Once machines can acquire all those abilities, they would be as good as humans at any new jobs too.
dropped.why: He argues that the historical pattern of creating new jobs could break if machines acquire every human ability. But that is conditional, he gives the 'historical scenario' (AI like steam or electricity) at least a 10% chance, and he calls for scenario planning because he is uncertain. He doesn't reject history as a guide outright.

dropped.quote: I cannot tell you whether the dynamism that results will be fundamentally good or fundamentally bad, though history tells me it will be good.
dropped.why: Hedged ('I cannot tell you whether ... good or ... bad'), and the same passage predicts that most thinking and doing will soon be done by machines, which is a break from the past. History is used only as a tiebreaker on whether the outcome is good, not as a guide to how AI will behave.

dropped.quote: I believe that AI will develop in a similar way.
dropped.why: The analogy is narrow: open-source Linux beating closed Unix, used to predict open versus closed AI models. It doesn't claim earlier general-purpose technologies are a guide to how AI behaves or how people will receive it.

dropped.quote: The reference class of prior technological transitions (agricultural revolution, printing press, industrialization) all feature regime changes to varying degrees.
dropped.why: He invokes the reference class, but only to argue that AI will bring regime change and state collapse, and the same theses say AI-native institutions will have little continuity with today's. Visitors will read 'hold' as 'AI is like past technologies'; he uses history to predict a radical break, which is a narrower and different claim.

dropped.quote: The tail-risk scenarios in which a tiny group leverages AGI to gain unprecedented power over everyone else in society and the world become less likely, because the rest of society will be more in the know about what’s happening.
dropped.why: The quote argues that transparency makes a small-group power grab less likely, and the line before it accepts that decisions 'will still be made by the same tiny group'. It is about transparency and power concentration, not about popular self-government as the basis of authority.

dropped.quote: It is perhaps obvious, but: as a society, we’ve decided democratic governments should control the military
dropped.why: The point is that democratic governments, not private CEOs, should control superintelligence. But his remedy is a national-security-state project with a 'sane chain of command', which is not popular self-government over experts and other unelected powers. He takes only part of the statement.

dropped.quote: Technology expands capabilities to people who wouldn't otherwise have them.
dropped.why: A narrower claim: tools widen access to capabilities, shown with website-builder and AI-avatar examples. It is not an on-balance judgment about market-driven technology. The passage has no clearly better line.

dropped.quote: Real innovation makes us more productive, but it also, I think, dignifies our workers. It boosts our standard of living.
dropped.why: He praises innovation for raising productivity and wages, but at once says the outcome 'depends on the purpose of our economic system' and sides with the populist critique of offshoring. He supports the technology side, not clearly the market-driven side.

dropped.quote: I am a big believer in the American private sector, and would almost never advocate for heavy government involvement in technology or industry.
dropped.why: The quote is about preferring the private sector to government in industry generally, not about whether technology serves people. The same passage also says he no longer applies that view to AGI. The passage has no clearly better line.

dropped.quote: First, it maps out a clear example of the positive outcomes that can result when the government embraces a pro-technology, pro-innovation perspective and views private-sector entrepreneurship as a strategic asset for achieving public good.
dropped.why: The quote praises government that backs innovation and private entrepreneurship, using GPS, a government-built system, as the example. That is a public-private claim, not a market-driven one. The passage has no clearly better line.

dropped.quote: The accelerationists have the long view of history on their side, and I broadly support the Andreesen vision of the future.
dropped.why: An indirect, hedged endorsement ('broadly support' someone else's vision), followed at once by 'nonetheless' and caveats about transition trade-offs and blowback. Markets aren't addressed. The passage has no clearly better line.

dropped.quote: And so to us, we wanted to call out certain maneuvers being done by the incumbents in AI as not what it may seem on the surface. We’re calling out how certain proposals might be useful for regulatory capture and how the doomer-ism mindset was maybe instrumental to those ends.
dropped.why: Heavily hedged ('might be useful', 'maybe instrumental'). It says incumbents' moves are 'not what it may seem', not plainly that leaders are dishonest about risks. The passage has no clearly better line.

dropped.quote: Instead, OpenAI’s governance structure failed in the November board crisis, and I lost trust in both the former board’s ability to govern and that OpenAI’s leadership was acting in good faith (violating Principle 8).
dropped.why: Narrower: he lost trust that OpenAI's leadership in particular was acting in good faith, after a governance crisis. That is not a claim about major AI leaders' honesty on risks in general. The passage has no clearly better line.

dropped.quote: Yes, the above measures are a big divergence from what corporations would want to do by default. Yes, they carry various costs, such as letting various bad actors find out about various things sooner.[8] However, the benefits are worth it, I think:
dropped.why: The measures he says are worth their costs are transparency commitments (public leaderboards, safety cases), mostly voluntary corporate pledges. This is not strict regulation, and the costs he names are not about deterring innovation.

dropped.quote: Regulation is often counterproductive, and naively “regulating AI” is more likely to cause harm than good.
dropped.why: He only says "naively" regulating AI does more harm than good. In the same essay he presses AI misalignment risk against Andreessen, so he does not oppose strict regulation as such.

dropped.quote: The federal government must act now to protect the public interest by putting in place limitations on facial recognition technology and measures for consent, privacy protections, meaningful transparency, and continuous oversight.
dropped.why: Covers only facial recognition (limits, consent, oversight). It is not about AI regulation broadly and does not address the innovation tradeoff.

dropped.quote: And I think we would have just a fundamentally different trajectory for AI as well, because the AI industry could have only manifested the way that it did on the backs of sloppy legislation and regulation.
dropped.why: A counterfactual about the past: she would have passed privacy and transparency laws before the boom. It leans reject but says nothing about strict regulation now or about innovation.

dropped.quote: We designed our society for excellence at strangling innovation. Now we’ve encountered a problem that can only be solved by a plucky coalition of obstructionists, overactive regulators, anti-tech zealots, socialists, and people who hate everything new on general principle.
dropped.why: The line is sarcastic: he concedes that society strangles innovation, then says AI needs obstructionists. The reject side is right on balance, but read alone the quote could seem to say regulation does harm.

dropped.quote: Surveillance capitalism knows too much to qualify for freedom. This is a rotten ideology at its core, and we must not be intimidated by it.
dropped.why: About surveillance capitalism's claim to market freedom in general (Toronto, Sidewalk Labs). It does not address AI regulation or innovation directly.

dropped.quote: Contrary to big tech executives’ cold-war style rhetoric about an arms race, what truly stifles innovation is the current arrangement where a few people build harmful technology and others constantly work to prevent harm
dropped.why: Argues that concentrated power, not regulation, is what stifles innovation. That leans reject, but she never says strict regulation would help or is harmless.

dropped.quote: Even if there were significant productivity gains from automation, these gains would not accrue directly to workers, and building shared prosperity by relying mainly on redistributive policies may not be feasible.
dropped.why: Hedged ('may not be feasible') and about relying mainly on redistribution in general, illustrated with minimum wages. He does not say direct distribution of wealth or ownership is unsound, only that it can't be the main strategy.

dropped.quote: Some people are excited by that notion— they’d welcome labs moving slowly and breaking nothing. These individuals are presumably in positions of privilege.
dropped.why: About tort liability regimes that would make labs risk-averse, not about deliberately slowing frontier AI. The line about people 'in positions of privilege' is also a jab at others rather than a statement of his own view. It leans reject, but a narrower question is being answered.

dropped.quote: Hence, it could be a great time to call for a slowdown in development.
dropped.why: Hedged ('it could be a great time to call for a slowdown'), and the reason given is a side point about bots polluting training data. The rest of the passage asks for sensible regulation (an off switch, accountability), not explicitly a slowdown.

dropped.quote: a coalition of democracies seeks to gain a clear advantage (even just a temporary one) on powerful AI by securing its supply chain, scaling quickly, and blocking or delaying adversaries’ access to key resources like chips and semiconductor equipment.
dropped.why: The 'entente strategy' quote is about democracies gaining an edge over autocracies. It doesn't address deliberately slowing frontier AI in general. Other passages in this same pack (Noah Smith, Warren, Kokotajlo, Murphy) say Amodei has called to 'pace the frontier' and slow capability progress, so the reject side may be backwards. Re-source this stance or drop it.

dropped.quote: We have 5 major American companies vigorously competing on frontier models. This brings out the best in everyone and helps America win the AI race.
dropped.why: Praises competition among five US labs and says doomer narratives were wrong, but never directly addresses deliberately slowing or stopping development. The side is implied, not stated.

dropped.quote: The solution is not to slow down technology, but rather to eliminate or reverse the excess incentives for automation over augmentation.
dropped.why: Said about automation and inequality: the fix for labor displacement is changing incentives, not slowing technology. He is not addressing slowing frontier AI for safety, which is how visitors will read the statement.

dropped.quote: The United States is resolved to stand at the forefront in developing and deploying frontier AI models and cutting edge AI applications
dropped.why: Says the US will stand at the forefront of frontier AI. That is a statement of ambition, not an explicit rejection of slowing. Elsewhere the US statement rejects centralized international control, which is also not quite the same question.

dropped.quote: You could bomb the data-centres, which — if they were developing superhuman AI — would be a good idea.
dropped.why: An off-the-cuff, conditional remark in an interview, which he immediately undercuts: bombing is futile 'unless you've changed your way of seeing', because 'they always get built again'. Showing the bombing line as his stance would likely draw a protest. He clearly opposes the AI project, but this quote is not a fair way to show it, and there is no better line in the text.

dropped.quote: At the same time if there is no other vector of growth in our society, we would be out of our minds not to take it.
dropped.why: About whether the US should embrace AI as a growth vector versus Europe. It is not about deliberately slowing frontier development, and the passage also lists his reservations about AI. The reject side is implied.

dropped.quote: Alexandria, along with three of my other books, was one of many thousands pirated by Amodei’s Anthropic corporation in one of the biggest acts of mass corporate copyright theft in history.
dropped.why: Calls Anthropic's training on his books piracy and theft 'with no permission', and welcomes the settlement. But he doesn't state a general rule that companies should have to pay; his pledge campaign is about refusing AI, not getting paid. Leans hold, and no clearer line is in the text.

dropped.quote: OpenAI joined a lobbying blitz aimed at helping the Trump administration push a 10-year moratorium on state lawmaking through Congress; it failed, but got an executive order aiming to do the same.
dropped.why: The quote only reports OpenAI's lobbying for a state-law moratorium. The passage casts that as an attack on democracy, so it leans hold, but Merchant never says outright that states should keep the power to make AI laws. No clearly better quote in the text.

dropped.quote: At the end of the essay, Marc advocates for free proliferation of open source AI. If the real threat from AI is that China catches up to American companies, then surely this is a bad idea.
dropped.why: A conditional rebuttal of Andreessen ('if the real threat is that China catches up, then surely this is a bad idea'). It leans reject, but it argues inside Marc's framing rather than stating Patel's own view outright.

dropped.quote: Second, I think we rightfully recognize that on the one hand, we want world-class models as products, and they should be proprietary.
dropped.why: He says world-class models as products should be proprietary, but in the same breath says open source is fundamentally necessary and that NVIDIA builds near-frontier open models. His view is mixed, not a clear reject.

dropped.quote: sometimes society will just not yet be pandemic-proof and it will be irresponsible to "democratize" biological weapon creation right away.
dropped.why: In the same sentence he says it is 'often reasonable' to release weights. He rejects only always releasing them, for example when society is not pandemic-proof. A reader could fairly see this as case-by-case rather than a reject.

dropped.quote: OpenAI is not about open source development — the technology needs to be developed and shaped for the right outcomes and safety.
dropped.why: Describes OpenAI's (early) approach of not doing open-source development, as a funder's endorsement. It is about one organisation's mission, not a general view on releasing the most capable models openly.

rewritten.was: AI product claims are shaped mainly to attract investors.
rewritten.now: Big AI companies like OpenAI now aim their products more at investors than at ordinary users.

rewritten.was: The main AI risk is powerful tools controlled by the largest corporations, not superintelligence.
rewritten.now: A pressing AI risk, whether or not AI becomes superintelligent, is that very powerful tools sit in the hands of the largest corporations, which face few checks.

rewritten.was: Foreign-policy experts have been overconfident; diplomacy with adversaries should be pursued to avoid escalation.
rewritten.now: Hawkish commentators have been overconfident about Ukraine, and the US should seriously try diplomacy with Russia given the risk of nuclear escalation.

rewritten.was: Independent, government-licensed private auditors should verify that frontier labs follow their safety plans.
rewritten.now: Frontier AI labs should be thoroughly audited against their own safety plans, probably by expert private bodies, possibly certified by government.

rewritten.was: Where technology goes is shaped by collective choices, especially public investment, not fixed in advance.
rewritten.now: The future of technology is not fixed in advance; through our collective investments in technology we choose among several possible futures.

rewritten.was: A high-bandwidth brain-computer link that lets humans merge with AI is the best long-term path for humanity.
rewritten.now: Merging with AI through a high-bandwidth brain interface is probably the best long-term outcome for humanity.

rewritten.was: Generative AI recombines existing human work creatively but has a ceiling set by its training data.
rewritten.now: Generative AI recombines existing human work in a real but limited way, and he suspects it cannot rise above what it was trained on.

rewritten.was: Human limits are part of human dignity, so efforts to transcend humanity through technology are mistaken.
rewritten.now: Human limits carry dignity, so trying to eliminate all human frailty through technology is dangerous, even though curing disease is good.

rewritten.was: Workplace AI surveillance without disclosure endangers workers and needs guardrails.
rewritten.now: Companies using AI without guardrails are getting workers surveilled, fired, hurt and even killed, so workplace AI needs guardrails.

rewritten.was: Government policy should protect startups from incumbents' regulatory capture.
rewritten.now: Bad government policy is now the biggest threat to tech startups, so defending them is a first-class political issue.

rewritten.was: Companies should build their own foundational technology so platform gatekeepers cannot limit what they make.
rewritten.now: Open ecosystems in AI matter so that companies are not boxed in by gatekeepers who control closed platforms.

rewritten.was: Corporate ethics principles cannot replace enforceable accountability, regulation and collective action.
rewritten.now: Corporate ethics codes and boards are no substitute for real accountability, public oversight and regulation.

rewritten.was: Any realistic theory of capitalism must account for sovereign power over property.
rewritten.now: Any serious account of capitalism has to use the idea of 'sovereign property', which he credits Moldbug with developing.

rewritten.was: AI is a highly useful everyday technology, and American hostility to it is out of step with the evidence.
rewritten.now: AI is an amazingly useful everyday technology, and Americans are unusually fearful of it compared with people in other countries.

rewritten.was: Since about 1970 technological progress has been fast in computing but slow in the physical world of energy, medicine and transport.
rewritten.now: Technological progress has been fast in computing and the internet but has stagnated in the physical world, such as transport and energy.

rewritten.was: Fear of the destructive potential of science after nuclear weapons helped produce decades of regulation and stagnation.
rewritten.now: Fear of science's destructive power after nuclear weapons is one underrated reason science and technology stagnated for decades.

rewritten.was: Democrats must not repeat globalization's neglect of working-class losers in the AI transition.
rewritten.now: Democrats must not repeat the mistake of globalization by letting AI erode working-class earnings and security.

rewritten.was: Liability rules and insurance are better tools than prohibitions for AI harms to outsiders and workers.
rewritten.now: Where AI failures could hurt outsiders, he says extending liability law and requiring insurance is plausibly the right fix, and he suggests job-loss insurance for workers.

rewritten.was: Frontier AI labs merit targeted government oversight, even though most proposed AI regulations are premature.
rewritten.now: Frontier AI labs merit targeted government oversight, even for those unsure most other AI regulation is useful.

rewritten.was: Training AI only on outcome rewards produces goal-driven agents that override norms, so alignment needs rule-following constraints.
rewritten.now: Training AI only on rewards for finished tasks tends to produce agents that override norms to reach goals; he thinks human rule-following may point toward a fix.

rewritten.was: Writers should now treat AI systems as a major audience for their work.
rewritten.now: He now writes largely with AI systems as his intended readers, expecting them to shape how he is remembered.

rewritten.was: Humans and AI are entering a symbiosis comparable to the evolutionary origin of complex cells.
rewritten.now: Humans and AI may be entering a symbiosis comparable to the evolutionary origin of complex cells.
